title: Mutable default arguments in functions

spans.text: WHY USE THIS?
A default expression is evaluated once when the function is defined. A mutable list, dict, or set can therefore become shared state across calls. Use a
None
sentinel and create a fresh object per call. If sharing is intentional, make it explicit rather than hiding it in a default.
CORE EXPLANATION
Python evaluates a default argument once, when the function is defined—not on every call. Thus a default such as
items=[]
is shared across calls and can retain earlier data. Use
None
as the default and create a fresh list inside the function. The same pitfall applies to mutable dictionaries and sets.
EXAMPLE CODE
QUESTION: What will this code print? Predict first, then run it.

spans.code:
def add_item(value: str, items: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(value)
    return items

print(add_item('a'))
print(add_item('b'))

spans.title: Warning
spans.text: Immutable defaults such as tuples and `None` are usually safe, but nested mutable values can still be shared.
